doc.title: Randy Sandke interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997

title: George Avakian and his Columbia productions
summary: Sandke praises Avakian's Columbia work and his return to the business with reissues and a JVC concert of unrecorded Armstrong compositions.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band

blocks.x: You had said some pretty kind words about George Avakian? That he gave you some good career boosts along the way. Or is it mostly just listening to his productions?

Well of course I grew up listening to a lot of the things that he did for Columbia, which is not only the reissues but the Miles Davis and Gil Evans. It was his idea to bring those two together. In fact he says he went to Miles and Miles had done all these quintet records and he said, “now that you’re with Columbia, we want to present you in a different way and like put you in a new direction, and we can get this budget together.” And he said, “why don’t you have somebody write something sort of big band or orchestrally, like Gunther Schuller or Gil Evans?” And of course Miles knew Gil and ended up picking Gil Evans. But George Avakian was very much a part of that. You know a lot of good — Sonny Rollins, Duke Ellington stuff, all kinds of things. But he was out of the business for a long — I mean I didn’t know if he was still alive or dead. And then just maybe six, seven years ago or something I was playing in a club and somebody brought him in. And I couldn’t believe how young he looked and I mean he was like in really good health and a really vital kind of guy. And I was just amazed. And I was talking about all those things

that he did. And he had really been kind of out of it so long and he didn’t have really good feelings about the record business, the way it had been run and the way it was being run. But since that time I mean I have to say he’s gotten back into it. He’s doing a lot of work for CBS-SONY with reissue projects. And then just recently this last June for the JVC festival we co-produced a concert which was this — he managed to find these Louis Armstrong compositions that Louis had never recorded, many of them written in his own hand, in the Library of Congress. So there was about eight or nine things that nobody knew was there, and hadn’t been heard. So we put on a concert where we played them, Nicholas Payton and myself. And then we did some Bix Beiderbecke things in the first half, and it got a lot of publicity and hopefully we’re going to make a record and do a tour next year.
